Last indexed: 1 February 2026 ( 1fda6b ) Overview Getting Started Core Client Architecture Error Handling Common Types and Usage Tracking Chat Completions Basic Chat Completion Streaming Chat Completion Messages and Content Types Multimodal Content Tool Calling and Function Definitions Structured Outputs with JSON Schema Reasoning and Chain-of-Thought Plugins: PDF Parser and Web Search Provider Routing and Fallbacks Prompt Caching Text Completions Embeddings Model Management API Key Management Generation Tracking JSON Schema Support Schema Generation from Go Types Schema Validation Examples and Recipes Testing and Development Reference Menu Prompt Caching Relevant source files api_keys.go chat.go chat_test.go client_test.go sample_prompt_test.go Overview Prompt caching is a feature that allows you to cache portions of your chat messages to reduce latency and costs for repeated API calls with similar content. When enabled, OpenRouter stores designated message parts in a cache, allowing subsequent requests to reuse this cached content instead of re-processing identical tokens. This feature is particularly valuable for use cases involving: Large system prompts that remain constant across multiple requests Long contextual documents (e.g., PDFs, knowledge bases) Multi-turn conversations where early messages don't change For information about multi-part message content structure, see Messages and Content Types . For general chat completion usage, see Basic Chat Completion . Sources: chat.go 453-455 Core Components Prompt caching is implemented through two primary types in the codebase: CacheControl Structure The CacheControl struct defines how caching should be applied to a message part: Field Type Description Type string Cache type - currently only supports "ephemeral" TTL *string Optional time-to-live in format "5m" or "1h" Integration with Message Parts Cache control is applied at the ChatMessagePart level, allowing fine-grained control over which portions of a message should be cached: Diagram: Cache Control Integration in Message Structure Sources: chat.go 450-460 chat.go 518-523 Cache Types Ephemeral Caching Currently, the only supported cache type is "ephemeral" , which stores cached content temporarily for subsequent requests using the same API key. Ephemeral caches are designed for short-term reuse patterns within a single session or workflow. The cache is not persisted long-term and may be evicted based on OpenRouter's cache management policies. Time-to-Live Configuration You can optionally specify a TTL to control how long content remains cached: Supported TTL formats: Minutes: "5m" , "10m" , "30m" Hours: "1h" , "2h" , "24h" Sources: chat.go 518-523 Request Flow with Caching Diagram: Caching Request Flow Sources: chat.go 615-642 client_test.go 163-208 Implementation Guide Basic Usage To enable prompt caching, you must use multi-part content format ( Content.Multi ) rather than simple text format ( Content.Text ): Important: Cache control cannot be applied when using Content.Text directly. You must use Content.Multi with ChatMessagePart elements. Is Implicit Caching Prompt Retention? Chris Clark · 10/23/2025 OpenRouter monitors every endpoint, from every provider, to understand their current data retention policy. We publish this in our API, in our docs, and support ZDR routing rules in our API. But data retention is not black and white; specifically Google has taken the stance (opens in new tab) that models with implicit prompt caching are in fact “retention”. Most providers would disagree – so we set out to form an independent opinion. What is implicit caching? Caching in general matters primarily because it can save an enormous amount of money. Every token an LLM generates depends on everything that came before it; recomputing those dependencies from scratch is wasteful. By caching (in a storage mechanism) the key and value tensors that represent the model’s intermediate activations (known as the “KV cache”) providers can skip prompt prefill and continue the conversation using much less compute. Implicit caching simply means that this cache is maintained automatically, behind the scenes, without explicit user control. Explicit caching accomplishes the same thing, but the user sets control headers around the sections of the prompt that they want the provider to cache. It’s explicit that the data is being stored for reuse. For that reason, explicit caching is never considered data retention. The question is whether implicit caching, which happens automatically within the inference system, should be treated as retention under Zero Data Retention (ZDR) standards. Three Tiers of Storage There are (roughly) three hierarchical tiers of storage & memory used for serving large models: On-device memory (HBM / GPU VRAM): This is where the active inference happens. Keys and values live here while tokens are being generated in real time. No controversy here; obviously the KV weights need to be loaded into the GPU for output generation.\ Host memory (CPU DRAM): When GPU memory fills up or context switches occur, the KV cache may spill over to host DRAM. In fact, many inference configurations are rapidly paging KV cache in and out of on-device memory between tokens so that each inference consumer gets a consistent stream of tokens back, without being blocked by a long generation. Again, this is volatile memory and no one would consider it “retention” of the prompt data. NVMe / SSD paging: The majority of commercial inference setups extend caching one step further, paging KV tensors to fast SSD storage via NVMe. This allows models to handle more concurrent sessions than the sum of their GPU and DRAM capacity would normally allow. This is, largely, where true “prompt caching” happens, and where the controversy resides. What’s in the box??? It should be the case that only the KV tensors (floating-point matrices that encode the result of pre-filling the prompt into the LLM) get paged out to the attached SSD. A one-way hash key from the incoming prompt is stored alongside the tensors, so that as new prompts come in a lookup can be performed to see if the precomputed KV cache can be loaded from the SSD. The token IDs or text fragments of the original prompts should not be stored alongside them. We have verified with the hyperscale clouds that host proprietary models that indeed no tokens or text are being paged out to SSDs. We have also validated this specifically with Groq and Cerebras (who, in fact, offer implicit caching but store everything in DRAM; no SSDs involved at all!). We have yet to find a provider that is paging text or tokens to SSDs, but intend on continuing this verification process for all providers. Lastly, it is worth noting that many more providers implement this SSD architecture, than the number who publicly offer cached pricing / implicit caching. This architecture of caching KV tensors makes the inference more efficient; providers are incentivized to implement it, and are not obligated to pass the savings on, or publicly offer lower prices for cached prompts.

The first fetch was too noisy. Let me try the canonical guide URL and the DeepWiki mirror for a cleaner read.

The OpenRouter docs page keeps coming back as a nav-heavy blob. Let me try the raw best-practices guide with a higher char limit, and also check for a dedicated features pageThe main docs are a JS-heavy SPA that fetches can't parse well. Let me grab the raw GitHub markdown and a TypeScript example insteadHere's the synthesis:

- **How it works** — OpenRouter supports explicit prompt caching via a `cache_control` field on message parts, with type `"ephemeral"` and an optional TTL (`"5m"`, `"1h"`, etc.). You must use multi-part content (not plain text) to tag which sections to cache — ideal for large system prompts, long documents, and multi-turn conversation prefixes. Cached tokens show up as `input_token_details.cache_read` in usage tracking, billed at a steep discount vs. fresh prefill. ([docs](https://openrouter.ai/docs/features/prompt-caching)) ([DeepWiki reference](https://deepwiki.com/reVrost/go-openrouter/4.10-prompt-caching))

- **Implicit vs. explicit caching** — OpenRouter draws a clear line: explicit caching (user-set `cache_control` headers) is never data retention. Implicit caching (provider-side KV tensors paged to ephemeral SSDs) is also treated as ZDR-compliant by OpenRouter, though Google disagrees for Gemini. KV caches are floating-point matrices — not recoverable text — and are cleared on session termination or eviction. ([blog post](https://openrouter.ai/announcements/is-implicit-caching-prompt-retention))

- **Model support & examples** — Supported models include `anthropic/claude-3-opus`, `google/gemini-2.5-flash`, and others listed in the docs. Runnable examples exist in the openrouter-examples repo for TypeScript + fetch, Vercel AI SDK v5, and Effect AI. Caching works with both sync and streaming requests; place cached content early in the message array for best performance. ([GitHub examples](https://github.com/OpenRouterTeam/openrouter-examples/tree/main/docs/prompt-caching.md)) ([TypeScript example](https://github.com/OpenRouterTeam/openrouter-examples/tree/main/typescript/fetch/src/prompt-caching/))

> Note: The canonical docs page at `openrouter.ai/docs/features/prompt-caching` is a JS-rendered SPA and couldn't be fetched as plain text — the DeepWiki mirror and GitHub examples filled the gap.
